nodes.claim: The cascade isn't gravity — it's a function of which side of the migration is doing the pulling. Flip the pull, and the cascade doesn't form.
nodes.why: The load-bearing claim of Part III. The cascade in Part II felt structural; this essay says the structure is contingent on a posture choice, not a physical law. Every inversion below is a way of flipping that pull.

nodes.claim: Operator-push → team-pull. The platform team publishes a skill; the receiving team installs and invokes it on their clock.
nodes.why: The first load-bearing flip. Same posture as Python 2to3, OpenRewrite, jscodeshift — producer authors once, consumer runs locally. What's new is shipping it as a skill the receiving team's agent already knows how to invoke.

nodes.claim: Single-shot → choreographed. A migration is a sequence of small reviewable PRs with state in the target repo, not one big diff.
nodes.why: The second flip. Spring Boot 2.7→3 is seven steps; each step is one PR a human will actually read. State in .migration-state.json lets the team pause and resume without losing position. 14-line diffs get reviewed; 700-line diffs don't.

nodes.claim: "Do the work" → teach while doing. Each step ships with publisher-authored prose that explains the transform before running it.
nodes.why: The author flags this one as the load-bearing inversion. The team ends each step with a working understanding of the transform — the next step is faster because they understood the first. Teaching is the part nobody else ships.

nodes.claim: Engine-only → engine + receiving-team UX. The codemods inside Bob are the same shape any AST tool produces; the contribution is the wrapper above.
nodes.why: The fourth flip. The engine layer (jscodeshift, OpenRewrite, ast-grep, Semgrep autofix, Codemod's CLI) is well-covered. The team-side surface — explain, pace, stop short of merge — is what's missing.

nodes.claim: bob-the-fixer is one instance of the artifact you get when you compose all four inversions — a Claude Code plugin shipping today.
nodes.why: The four flips compose. Bob is one shape that holds them all simultaneously. The four migrations shipped at first publish — migrate-spring-boot-3, migrate-junit-4-to-5, migrate-jest-to-vitest, adopt-structured-logging — are concrete instances of the composed shape.

nodes.claim: Before the agent-skills format, the operator had no way to ship anything but a PR. Skills are the second option.
nodes.where: why this couldn't have shipped earlier
nodes.why: Names the mechanism behind why team-pull is suddenly deliverable at scale. Runbooks get skimmed; CLIs get forgotten; CI bots open PRs. SKILL.md + plugin marketplace is the first format where 'here is a migration with the teacher built in' is one install command.

nodes.claim: Across surveyed AI coding tools as of May 2026 — Cursor, Continue, Aider, Cody, JetBrains, Copilot, Sweep, Windsurf, Codemod's CLI — none ship the active teaching layer.
nodes.why: The empirical observation behind the load-bearing inversion. The author's surveyed claim — open to falsification by anyone who finds a counter-example. If a surveyed tool does ship a teaching-while-doing surface, this node moves.

nodes.claim: Python 2to3 — single command, run locally on the team's clock, ships with the standard library since Python 3.
nodes.why: Earliest published instance of the team-pulled posture. The producer (CPython core) authored once; consumers ran on their own clock. Grounds S02.

nodes.claim: OpenRewrite OSS — Java migration recipes distributed via Maven Central; teams pull, run, commit.
nodes.why: Mature Java-ecosystem instance of the team-pulled engine. Recipes are the producer's contribution; running them is the consumer's. Grounds S02 and S05 — well-covered engine layer that doesn't include the team-side teaching surface.

nodes.claim: jscodeshift — Facebook's JS codemod toolkit; treats codemods as a library devs run on their own clock.
nodes.why: Engine-layer prior art, JavaScript ecosystem. The codemods inside Bob's steps are the same shape any AST tool produces; jscodeshift is one place that shape was first packaged for OSS use. Grounds S05.

nodes.claim: Shopify (2020): "A single centralized team can't make change happen by working against the momentum of hundreds of developers." Pivoted to Architecture Guild + embedded engineers + team-installed Packwerk.
nodes.why: Clearest published statement of the anti-push thesis as a strategic position. Bob's posture (team-pulled, team-paced) is in the same direction in a different shape (Claude Code skill rather than static-analysis library). Grounds S01.

nodes.claim: Codemod ships the engine and Campaigns — operator-side fan-out across N repos. A real product, well-funded engine layer; the team-side teacher isn't in their offering.
nodes.why: Closest contemporary in the space — kudos to the team. The engine and operator-side orchestration are mature; this is an invitation, not a contest. If Codemod ships a team-paced + teaching-layer surface, the field is better for it.

nodes.claim: Anthropic SKILL.md (folder + YAML frontmatter, on-demand load) + plugin marketplace — the distribution channel that makes "a migration with a teacher built in" one install command for the receiving team.
nodes.why: Names the substrate that turned the team-pulled model from runbook-shaped into installable-skill-shaped. Grounds D07 — skills are why this couldn't have shipped earlier.

nodes.claim: Hyrum Wright's Large-Scale Changes (Software Engineering at Google, Ch 22): LSCs at Google almost always machine-generated; pre-LLM operator-side practice for cross-cutting change.
nodes.why: Historical anchor for the operator-push path Bob is inverting. The LSC pattern shipped at Google scale via codemod; the cascade Part II names is what happens when the same pattern runs against a fleet of teams that didn't author the change. Grounds the cascade-as-failure-mode framing implicit in S01.

eyes.what: The surveyed-tools claim — "none of Cursor, Continue, Aider, Cody, JetBrains, Copilot, Sweep, Windsurf, Codemod's CLI ship an active teaching layer as of May 2026" — is the author's hand survey. Falsifiable but not yet externally corroborated.
eyes.why: The load-bearing observation behind S04 (teach-while-doing). Open to falsification by anyone who finds a counter-example in the surveyed set, or names a tool that wasn't surveyed. Worth a follow-up pass each quarter; the field is moving fast.

eyes.what: Teaching-as-load-bearing is the author's framing. Adjacent literature (literate programming, dev-experience research, runbook-vs-skill comparisons) names the value of explanation alongside execution but does not frame the teaching layer as the load-bearing inversion in cross-cutting change.
eyes.why: The framing reads cleanly against the surveyed tools, but a published taxonomy already naming "teaching-while-doing" as the missing primitive would let the essay sit alongside it instead of re-naming it. Active eyes — most likely place an external reader could already have shipped the same claim.

eyes.what: Bob is presented as one demonstration of the four-inversion shape. The claim that the four inversions are jointly sufficient to defeat the cascade is implicit, not yet proven against a second instance.
eyes.why: One artifact is an existence proof for the shape, not for the shape's necessity or sufficiency. Other shapes that hold the same four inversions — or that drop one and still avoid the cascade — would sharpen the claim. Open invitation to the field.

actions.label: Install bob
actions.body: Watch the choreography land. Install, invoke, one step, stop. Demonstrates the team-pulled posture and per-step pacing in 90 seconds.

actions.label: Teaching layer
actions.body: Same diff. With and without the explanation wrapped around it. Drills the load-bearing inversion — S04.

actions.label: Pull vs push
actions.body: Two scenarios land in your week as team lead. Pick the response. Drills S02.

actions.label: Author one step
actions.body: Write the rename rule. Run it against the fixture. Drills S05 — what shipping a step actually feels like.

actions.label: Pick one cross-cutting change you tried to push
actions.body: What would the team-pulled shape have looked like? Where would the per-step pacing have lived? What's the teaching layer your PR description didn't carry?

actions.label: Try bob
actions.body: If you have a Spring Boot 2.7, JUnit 4, Jest, or unstructured-logging codebase, install the plugin and run the migration. The repo is MIT-licensed and under 1,000 lines.

rubric.note: Each load-bearing claim cites a real prior-art reference; the four inversions are explicitly framed as a recombination, not an invention. Composite is mid not strong because the surveyed-tools observation (O08) and the four-inversions-are-sufficient claim (D06) are author-side surveys without independent corroboration yet.
rubric.soft:
Two soft spots:
1. The surveyed-tools claim is the load-bearing empirical observation but rests on the author's hand survey. A reproducible methodology — feature matrix across the named tools, last-checked date, link to each tool's docs section that confirms or denies a teaching layer — would let a reader verify rather than trust.
2. "The four inversions compose" presents as an exhaustive decomposition. It may not be. There are plausible fifth axes — reversibility, blast radius, telemetry — that the essay doesn't surface. Worth marking the four as the ones bob explicitly inverts rather than the complete set.
